title: Altimetrik Opens Healthcare and Life Sciences AI Centre in Hyderabad
excerpt: The AI engineering company's new Center of Excellence launches PharmaOS, a framework of more than 35 agents promising a validated life-sciences workflow in one week.
body:
• Altimetrik opened a Healthcare and Life Sciences Center of Excellence in Hyderabad on 16 October 2026, inside its 22,000 sq ft Phoenix Equinox office in Gachibowli.
  • The centre’s first offering is PharmaOS, an agentic AI framework with more than 35 agents and accelerators for clinical, regulatory, manufacturing and commercial work.
  • Altimetrik says PharmaOS can take a client from a defined concept to a validated, governed AI workflow in one week.
  • The Hyderabad office is home to more than 300 Altimetrik employees; the launch follows a Pune expansion that took the global workforce past 10,000, the company said.

Altimetrik, an AI engineering company, has opened a Healthcare and Life Sciences Center of Excellence in Hyderabad, placing a dedicated life-sciences AI unit next to the pharmaceutical companies and contract research organisations whose workflows it wants to automate. The centre, announced on 16 October, sits inside Altimetrik’s 22,000 sq ft office at Phoenix Equinox in Gachibowli, near HITEC City, which the company says is home to more than 300 of its employees.

Its first product is PharmaOS, an agentic AI framework built on Altimetrik’s ALTi AIOS operating system. According to the company’s announcement, PharmaOS brings together more than 35 purpose-built agents and accelerators spanning commercial operations, clinical and regulatory evidence review, manufacturing and quality, responsible AI and data modernisation.

"Hyderabad's deep pharma expertise and technology talent make it the right home for this Center, bringing together the capabilities needed to deliver practical, industry-specific innovation."

— Raj Sundaresan, Chief Executive Officer, Altimetrik

What PharmaOS is built to do

The pitch is speed with governance. Altimetrik says the centre can take a client from a defined concept to a validated, governed agentic workflow in one week, given a defined business challenge, agreed data access and a bounded workflow. Tasks named in the announcement and in Hindu BusinessLine’s report include reviewing clinical study reports, GxP compliance checks and batch-release readiness. Outputs are traced to source evidence, and people remain responsible for decisions — a design the company presents as essential in a regulated industry where an untraceable AI output has little value.

PharmaOS is designed to work with AI ecosystems from Google, Anthropic and OpenAI, with model flexibility in the underlying architecture, both reports said. The one-week model builds in security, observability, source traceability, quality checks, human decision rights and a measurable business KPI from the outset, so a client can judge a workflow in its real enterprise context before committing to a wider rollout.

Why Hyderabad

Hyderabad is one of India’s main pharmaceutical and life-sciences clusters, with drug makers, vaccine producers and contract research firms concentrated around Genome Valley and the western IT corridor. Altimetrik said it chose the city to be close to the companies whose workflows will shape its offerings, and to draw on its pool of clinical, regulatory, quality and engineering specialists. The centre will support work across drug discovery, clinical development, commercial operations, manufacturing, patient engagement and care delivery.

The launch also extends Altimetrik’s India footprint. The company said a recent expansion in Pune took its global workforce past 10,000 — BusinessLine put the figure past 11,000 — and that the Hyderabad centre expands the role of its India teams in global AI engineering delivery. BusinessLine reported the centre would support life-sciences workflows for global clients from the Phoenix Equinox site.

What happens next

Altimetrik says more offerings will be built alongside clients after PharmaOS, rather than launched as finished products. That co-creation model will be the test of the centre: whether pharmaceutical firms entrust regulated workflows — evidence review, compliance and batch release — to AI agents built in a week, and whether the traceability and human-oversight claims hold up in audits. For Hyderabad, the centre adds another specialised AI employer to a corridor already competing for engineers who understand both software and regulated science.
